name: Mmen
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Björkestedt, Lena 2011. A Phonological Sketch of the Mmen Language (SIL Cameroon); Agha, Grace Beh 1987. Phonology of Mmen (MPI pure.mpg.de item_403515, HTTP 403)

new_statements.quote: Some important features like vowel length and tone will be examined in this chapter. Mmen like Aghem or many other Western grassfields languages is a tone language. It is a language in which both segmental and pitch phonemes, otherwise known as tones, go into the composition of words. It is known that in tone languages, words could either be distinguished on the basis of segments or/and tones; Mmen is no exception. The tones attested in the language are in some cases contrastive. [p. 67] … There are principally five tones in Mmen namely – the high tone – the mid tone – the low tone – the rising tone – the falling tone. [p. 67] … Each syllable carries one of the five contrastive tones above mentioned occurring in the language. [p. 68]
new_statements.citation: Agha, Grace Beh. 1987. Phonology of Mmen. Mémoire de Maîtrise, Université de Yaoundé, Department of African Languages and Linguistics. 80 pp. Chapter Three, 'Suprasegmental phonology'.
new_statements.locator: p. 67 (pdf p. 73), ch. III opening; p. 68 (pdf p. 74), §III.2.1 'Phonemic tone contrast'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mmen is described as a tone language: every syllable bears one of five contrastive tones (H, M, L, rising LH, falling HL); the suprasegmental chapter treats vowel length and tone only and makes no statement about word stress or accent. No source examined (Agha 1987; Bangha 2003; Möller 2012; Nilsson 2013; Chiatoh 1993) mentions stress at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: rising and falling tones are rare (about one percent of vocabulary, p. 68) and the rising tone is in some cases non-contrastive (p. 69); Möller 2012:6 notes surface M whose contrastiveness needs more research.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable level: tones assigned per syllable, described from words cited in isolation (Agha 1987) and in a 'same X' frame (Möller 2012). Nilsson 2013 stresses that her tone marks are surface pitches of citation forms, not underlying tones.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Mmen of Bafumen (Bafmen/Bafmeng), Fungom Subdivision, Menchum Division, NW Cameroon — Glottolog language-level mmen1238 (ISO bfm), Center/Central Ring Grassfields Bantu; Agha 1987 calls it a 'Western grassfields' language. No dialect is singled out; Troyer et al. 1995 (not fetched sources) is the dialect survey.

sources.note: Introductory phonology sketch §1.8 (consonant and vowel charts) and §1.8.3 'Tones' (thesis p. 21, pdf p. 31): 'Like other African languages, Mmen is a tone language' … five tones (three level, two contour). No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Nilsson, Signe. 2013. Space and time in Mmen: a Central Ring Grassfields Bantu language. BA thesis, General Linguistics, Lund University (LUP 3602318); also issued as Locative prepositions in Space and Time: Mmen Language. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon (SIL L&C Archives 61354), 61 pp.
sources.note: §1.3.4 'Mmen language structure' (p. 10) summarises Björkestedt 2011a:44: 27 consonants, 9 vowels, nine phonetic pitches on isolated syllables (H, M, L, HL, HM, ML, LM, MH, low-falling); 'm' can be tone-bearing as the cl. 6a prefix. No mention of stress or accent anywhere. Reference list gives Björkestedt 2011a/b as Yaoundé: CABTAL and Kießling 'Mmen tonology' / 'A Sketch of Mmen' as unpublished MSS.

sources.citation: Möller, Mirjam. 2012. The noun and verb in Mmen: a Center Ring Grassfields Bantu language. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon / Ministry of Scientific Research and Innovation. 47 pp. (SIL L&C Archives 52745; PDF fetched sources via Wayback)
sources.note: §3 Phonology (pp. 3-8): 26 consonants, 9 vowels; §3.2.1 'Tone within the noun' gives at least four underlying root melodies H, L, HL, LH plus surface M; refers to Björkestedt 2011a for the fuller phonology. 'Accent' occurs only as 'accent marks' for tone. Nothing on stress.
